prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(2,-3,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6(x-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,-3).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,-3) & =6(2-1)=6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,-3) & ={f}_{x}(2,-3)(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6x-12 \\ z & =6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-3 \\ z=6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=-3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=6x-9$ (or $6x-z-9=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨6,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨6,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-6⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-6⟩=⟨1,0,6⟩$ is also parallel to it.

full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,-1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,0) & =\frac{(-1)(0-(-1))}{2(-1)(0+1)} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,0) & ={f}_{y}(-1,0)(y-0) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $y-2z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,-2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2\,j+k \\  & =⟨0,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,2,1⟩.$

prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$

prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & ={f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0)(y-0) \\ z-2 & =-\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2j+k \\  & =⟨0,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-2,1⟩.$

prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

prompt: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
full_worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.
